title.narrative: WFP - UNICEF Joint Programme on Social Protection in Uganda 2019-2024
WFP - UNICEF gemensamt program social trygghet i Uganda 2019-2024

description.narrative:
The overall objective of the programme was to achieve improved health and nutrition of young children and enhanced community and household resilience among refugees and host populations in refugee-hosting districts of West Nile.
The overall objective is broken down into three specific programme objectives:
- Improved economic inclusion of households - for households to enhance their participation in local economies by increasing their contribution to and benefits from markets - Improved maternal and child nutrition status - Improved maternal, neonatal and child health
These objectives are broken down in a number of outcomes on both beneficiary and system levels.
Outcome 1.1 - Increased or more secure incomes Outcome 1.2 - Improved access to markets Outcome 1.3 - Improved dietary variation of households Outcome 1.4 - Improved access to health and nutrition services Outcome 1.5 - Improved health seeking behaviour Outcome 2.1 - More efficient, transparent, child- and nutrition-sensitive social protection systems. Outcome 2.2 - More efficient, transparent, child- and nutrition sensitive health services
The programme was to deliver a number of outputs in order to achieve the outcomes and overall objectives.
- Support links with on-going Social Protection Programmes - Provide child sensitive household transfers - Support cash transfer mechanisms - Support beneficiary information and assistance management (BIAM) - Support retail markets - Support to feedback and complaints systems - Health system strengthening and support - Social Behaviour Change Communication for increased demand for health services
There was also a component on operational research for continuous learning and improvement of social and health services.

WFP i samarbete med UNICEF har ansökt till Sida om 477 000 000 SEK (49 499 474 USD) i stöd för att genomföra programmet "Child-Sensitive Social Protection in Refugee-Hosting Districts of West Nile, Uganda" under perioden 2019-2024.
Programmet syftar till ökad motståndskraft och social trygghet, förbättrad hälsa och nutrition för utsatta barn och mödrar i West Nile i norra Uganda.
Den övergripande inriktningen på programmet är att stärka och komplettera existerande nationella program och system för social trygghet och hälsa med fokus på att göra dessa system mer effektiva och mer inriktade på att motverka barns utsatthet och främja bättre nutrition. Programmet förväntas göra pågående stöd mer hållbara och ta tillvara synergier genom att utnyttja resurser från befintliga nationella program, basservice och system för att nå starkare resultat för resiliens, hälsa och nutrition.
Programmets övergripande mål är stärkt ekonomisk inkludering av hushåll, förbättrad hälsa och nutrition för mödrar och barn. Det är inriktat på nexus mellan humanitärt stöd och långsiktigt utvecklingssamarbete genom att stärka införlivandet av flyktingar i existerande nationella system för hälsa och social trygghet.
Programmet syftar till att nå effekter på två nivåer; direkt för målgruppen, samt på systemnivå. Effekter på systemnivå förväntas uppnås genom att programmet bidrar till mer effektiva och transparenta system för social trygghet och hälsa med stärkt barn-perspektiv och ökad nutritionskänslighet.
Stödet till systemnivå länkas till pågående program för social trygghet (såsom SAGE - Social Assistance Grants for Empowerment, NUSAF3 - Northern Uganda Social Assistance Fund och DRDIP - Development Response to Displacement Impacts Project) och förväntas åtgärda brister i systemen för hälsovård och social trygghet.
Dialoginsatser riktade till målgruppen ska stärka efterfrågan på hälsovård och bidra till förändrat beteende som stärker resiliens, hälsa och nutrition.
De planerade effekterna för målgruppen är: - Ökad eller mer tillförlitlig inkomst genom kontantstöd - Förbättrad tillgång till marknader med lägre priser och högre variation på livsmedel - Mer varierad diet för hushållen - Förbättrad tillgång till kvalitativ hälsovård - Förbättrad efterfrågan på hälsovård
Programmet administreras av WFP genom ett standardavtal "Standard Administrative Agreement (SAA) for joint UN programmes" och implementeras av WFP och UNICEF i samarbete med lokala aktörer och ansvariga ministerier för social trygghet och hälsa. Det systemstärkande stödet bygger på pågående insatser av UNICEF och WFP för att stärka hälsosystemet, ge humanitärt stöd till flyktingar och stärka systemet för social trygghet. Det föreslagna stödet kompletterar pågående humanitärt stöd från WFP till flyktingar och bidrar till att utveckla mer hållbara lösningar i den långvariga humanitära situationen. Pågående stöd från UNICEF för att stärka hälsosystem och hälsotjänster kommer att införlivas i det föreslagna programmet som kommer vara mer integrerat och holistiskt.
En ny aspekt i programmet är komponenten för social trygghet med förmedling av kontantstöd till mottagare. Det förväntas bidra till effektiv fattigdomsminskning för sårbara hushåll och ge en förbättrad situation för både flyktingar och värdbefolkning vilket kan minska spänningar i dessa samhällen där risken för konflikt över otillräckliga resurser och samhällsservice har ökat efter det stora flyktingmottagandet. Programmet syftar också till påverka marknader för att öka tillgång till och variation av näringsrika varor till lägre priser.
Jämställdhetsperspektivet integreras tydligt i insatsen och en fördjupad analys kommer göras under det första året av kopplingen mellan jämställdhet, funktionshinder, hälsa och nutrition i de valda distrikten.
Programmet genomförs med en flexibel ansats där genomförandet utvecklas och anpassas i nära samarbete med nyckelaktörer i statliga strukturer på nationell och lokal nivå för att säkerställa hållbarhet. Den integrerade insatsen där WFP och UNICEF samarbetar förväntas också bidra till ökad effektivitet, kvalitet och långsiktig hållbarhet.
Stödet till systemen för social trygghet och hälsovård kompletteras av implementeringsforskning som både stödjer genomförandet av programmet och bidrar till kvalitativt, evidensbaserat, lärande. Detta förväntas bidra till att stödja den långsiktiga utvecklingen av systemen för social trygghet och hälsovård i Uganda.

WFP in cooperation with UNICEF has applied to Sida for 477 000 000 SEK (49 499 474 USD) to support implementation of the programme "Child-Sensitive Social Protection in Refugee-Hosting Districts of West Nile, Uganda" during the period 2019-2024. The programme aims to achieve increased resilience and social protection, improved health and nutrition for vulnerable children and mothers in West Nile. It has a focus on the nexus between humanitarian support and long-term development cooperation through strengthening the inclusion of refugees in existing national systems for health and social protection. The overarching philosophy of the programme is to not create new programmes and systems, but to strengthen and complement existing, national social protection and health programmes and systems with a strong focus on making such systems more efficient and effective and more child- and nutrition-sensitive. This approach seeks not only to make program results sustainable, but also to help leverage the efforts and resources of these national programmes, services and systems to achieve enhanced results, in particular in terms of resilience, health and nutrition.The programme objectives are improved economic inclusion of households, improved maternal and child nutrition and improved maternal and child health. Programme outcomes are pursued at two levels; the level of direct beneficiaries of programme activities and the level of systems. The programme aims to affect the systems level through achieving more efficient, transparent, child- and nutrition-sensitive social protection systems as well as more efficient child- and nutrition-sensitive health systems. The systems-strengthening support will link to ongoing social protection programmes (such as SAGE, Social Assistance Grants for Empowerment, NUSAF3, Northern Uganda Socail Assistance Fund, DRDIP, Development Response to Displacement Impacts Project) and will cover essential gaps in current health care and social protection systems.Behavioural change communication directed to beneficiaries will support increased demand for services and changed behaviour that improves resilience, health and nutrition.The outcomes for targeted beneficiaries will be:- Increased or more secure income, through cash transfers- Improved access to markets, with lower prices and higher diversity - Improved dietary diversity- Improved access to quality health services- Improved health-seeking behaviourThe new aspect of the programme is the social protection component with direct cash transfers to beneficiaries. This component is expected to add to efficient poverty reduction for vulnerable households and to provide an improved situation for both refugees and the refugee hosting population which can decrease tension in these societies where the risk for conflicts over insufficient resources and services has increased after the refugee influx. The programme also aims to affect markets to achieve increased availability and diversity of essential goods at lower prices.The gender perspective is clearly integrated in the programme and an in-depth analysis will be undertaken during the first year of the linkages between gender, disability, health and nutrition in the selected districts. The programme will be implemented through a flexible approach, where implementation will be developed and adapted in close collaboration with key actors in existing government structures at national and local level to ensure sustainability. The integrated approach combining efforts of WFP and UNICEF is also expected to improve efficiency, quality and long-term sustainability.

title.narrative: Avtal - 11739 WFP-UNICEF Gemensamt program social trygghet i Uganda
Beslut om större ändring av insats

description.narrative:
Expected Results
1.WFP-led Component Improved Household Resilience, Women's Economic Empowerment and Child Nutrition
The NutriCash Cash Plus approach significantly improved child nutrition while strengthening household resilience and women's economic empowerment. The component exceeded implementation targets (102 percent) and reached 13,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women and caregivers of children under two through predictable cash transfers combined with nutrition education, financial literacy and livelihood support. Approximately 90 percent of transfers were spent on food, contributing to improved household food security and dietary diversity. The impact evaluation found an 8.9 percentage point reduction in child stunting, demonstrating that integrating cash assistance with behaviour change and nutrition interventions can effectively reduce chronic malnutrition during the critical first 1,000 days of life.
The programme also strengthened households' capacity to withstand future shocks. Financial literacy reached 15,102 beneficiaries, while approximately USD 1.2 million was mobilised through mandatory savings and reinvested into productive activities. Backyard gardening training reached 13,882 households, with 92 percent establishing household gardens, improving year-round access to nutritious foods and reducing dependence on markets. Increased uptake of antenatal care, iron supplementation, malaria prevention, deworming and family planning further contributed to improved maternal and child health outcomes.
2. UNICEF-led Component Strengthened Maternal, Newborn and Child Health Systems
The programme substantially strengthened maternal, newborn and child health services, improving survival and the quality of care for refugee and host populations. Investments in High Dependency Units and Neonatal Intensive Care Units across 10 hospitals contributed to saving an estimated 4,111 mothers with severe obstetric complications and nearly 49,000 newborns, significantly expanding access to life-saving emergency care.
Nutrition and primary healthcare services also improved considerably. Treatment for severe acute malnutrition reached 34,982 children, more than double the programme target, while 6.2 million children received Vitamin A supplementation. Investments in water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure improved service quality in 48 health facilities, benefiting approximately 865,000 people. In addition, nearly 7,000 Village Health Teams were integrated into national health information systems, strengthening community-level service delivery, surveillance and continuity of care. Together, these investments increased the resilience and capacity of Uganda's public health system beyond the lifetime of the programme.
3. Cross-cutting Component Stronger Community Systems and Sustainable Government Capacity
The programme strengthened community systems to support the sustainable delivery of child-sensitive social protection. More than 1,200 Mother Care Groups were established, providing effective platforms for nutrition counselling, behaviour change communication, financial literacy and referrals to health services. These groups strengthened linkages between vulnerable households and essential public services while promoting community ownership of nutrition and social protection outcomes.
The programme also made substantial investments in strengthening national systems and institutional capacity. Uganda's National Single Registry was upgraded to integrate data on more than 4.1 million beneficiaries across ten social protection management information systems, significantly improving beneficiary identification, coordination and programme efficiency. Government capacity was further enhanced through the training of more than 2,300 government officials and the certification of 13 national Master Trainers using the TRANSFORM social protection curriculum. Together, these investments strengthened government ownership and established a more robust institutional foundation for scaling integrated social protection beyond West Nile.
Unexpected Results
The programme generated stronger women's economic empowerment than originally anticipated. The impact evaluation found a 12.4 percentage point increase in women's ownership and control of productive assets, strengthening their influence over household decisions related to food security, nutrition and livelihood investments.
Many households used cash transfers to build long-term resilience rather than only meeting immediate consumption needs. Approximately 54 percent of beneficiary households invested in productive assets, including poultry (43 percent) and small livestock (11 percent), creating additional income sources and strengthening their capacity to cope with future shocks. In several communities, these assets multiplied over time, demonstrating sustained livelihood benefits beyond the programme period.
Programme benefits extended beyond direct beneficiaries through community-led learning and stronger government ownership. Beneficiaries voluntarily shared knowledge on nutrition, backyard gardening and financial management with neighbouring households, while investments in national systems and institutional capacity strengthened the foundation for greater government ownership and long-term sustainability of social protection programmes.
